We are unable to determine what is visible within the interior.
Prior Research and Theories
Previously, Coastal Sensing & Survey had classified this target as LU001. Described as a Barge.

Shipwreck City Data
This target has been classified as a wood shipwreck resting in 40 feet of water and measuring roughly 25 feet by 8 feet. The shipwreck rests upright on the lakebed, with much of the hull structure still present with minor places of deterioration. Visible features include partial hull markings, exposed wooden structural members, and a circular opening within the wreck that may represent one of the craft’s gun wells. Additional unidentified debris is visible within the hull. This shipwreck is believed to be a Landing Craft, Vehicle, Personnel (LCVP), commonly known as a Higgins Boat.

Previously, Coastal Sensing & Survey had classified this target as LU06. Described as a weed-covered landing craft. DCS Films had classified this target as an LCVP, or Higgins Boat. Described as bearing the partial hull number "PA 201," possibly connecting the craft to the USS Menard, though the complete designation could not be determined. Previously, Lake Union Virtual Museum had classified this target as a Higgins Boat. Described as a landing craft.

Type: Vessel | Class: Barge Wreck | Subclass: Wooden
Shipwreck City Data
This target has been classified as a wood barge wreck resting in 15 feet of water and measuring roughly 91 feet by 26 feet. The barge wreck rests upright on the lakebed, with substantial portions of the wooden hull and deck structure still present. Visible features include large deck beams, substantial structural timbers, several upright structural members extending above the wreck, and multiple openings that provide views into the interior. Additional debris is visible within the hull. This barge wreck has been positively identified as Foss 54 (YC 191).
Prior Research and Theories
Previously, Coastal Sensing & Survey had classified this target as LU07. Described as the wreck of a Foss barge, though an earlier CSS entry identifies the barge as Foss #74, creating a discrepancy within the source record. DCS Films had classified this target as Foss 54. Described as the former U.S. Navy barge YC 191, with historical photographs and additional information documenting the vessel's history and specifications. Lake Union Virtual Museum had identified this target as Foss 54. Described as the wreck of Foss barge #54 in Lake Union.
Additional Context
Foss 54 was originally built in 1908 for the U.S. Navy in Bremerton, Washington, as YC 191. Historical data tells us that the barge carried coal, lumber, and other materials in the Puget Sound region over a working life spanning several decades. Its documented history becomes uncertain around 1969, and the exact circumstances and date of its sinking remain unclear. Shipwreck City is actively researching this vessel's history and will provide more details as we learn more.

Shipwreck City Data
This target has been classified as a wood shipwreck, resting in 40 feet of water and measuring roughly 55 feet by 14 feet. The shipwreck rests upright on the lakebed and survives primarily in two separated sections, with much of the midship structure broken apart. Visible features include outer hull planking, exposed ribs and framing, deck beams and planking, rectangular openings within the surviving superstructure, a diamond-shaped metal plate with a central fastener along the hull, and two large deck cleats. The wreck is identified as the Kahlenberg.

Prior Research and Theories
Previously, Coastal Sensing & Survey had classified this target as LU12. Described as the wreck of the Kahlenberg. DCS Films had classified this target as Target 13, Kahlenberg. Described as an identified Lake Union wreck with documented U.S. Navy service and later civilian use.

Additional Context
The Kahlenberg was built in 1913 as a wooden vessel approximately 50 feet long and 11 feet wide. Historical research describes the vessel as serving with the U.S. Navy as a tender before later being used by Kahlenberg Industries as a demonstration vessel. Captain Franz Nelson later brought the vessel to Puget Sound, where it was used in the local commercial shrimp fishery. Shipwreck City is actively researching this vessel's history and will provide more details as we learn more.

Type: Vessel | Class: Shipwreck | Subclass: Wood
Shipwreck City Data
This target has been classified as a wood shipwreck, resting in 40 feet of water and measuring roughly 90 feet by 18 feet. The shipwreck rests upright on the lakebed, with much of the wooden hull and deck structure still intact and several areas opened or deteriorated enough to expose the interior. Visible features include outer hull planking, deck planking, several rectangular deck openings, exposed internal framing, and a prominent H-shaped timber bitt consisting of two upright posts joined by a heavy crosspiece. The wreck has been identified as the J.E. Boyden.

Prior Research and Theories
Previously, Coastal Sensing & Survey had classified this target as LU42. Described as the wreck of the J.E. Boyden. DCS Films had classified this target as the J.E. Boyden. Described as a wooden tug measuring approximately 85 feet long with a 19-foot beam. Lake Union Virtual Museum had classified this target as the J.E. Boyden. Described as a wooden tug, with documentation noting painted name lettering on the hull and an H-shaped timber bitt associated with the vessel’s towing equipment.

Additional Context
The J.E. Boyden was built in Seattle in 1888 and operated as a wooden steam tug. During its working life, the tug was used to tow sailing vessels, barges, and other maritime traffic throughout the region. The vessel transported or towed materials including coal, lumber, ore, railcars, and log booms. The J.E. Boyden remained in service for several decades before being abandoned in Lake Union in 1935. Its exact date of sinking is not presently known, though likely to be in 1935. Shipwreck City is actively researching this vessel's history and will provide more details as we learn more.

Type: Debris | Class: Plane Wreck | Subclass: Metal
Shipwreck City Data
This target has been classified as metal debris, resting in 40 feet of water and measuring roughly 12 feet in length. The object has been identified as an aircraft drop tank. It lies on its side and is partially settled into the lakebed and has sustained significant damage and is broken in the middle. A prominent horizontal seam runs along the tank's midline, and there is a circular fitting near the damaged section. The seam is consistent with the joined halves used in the construction of aircraft drop tanks, while the circular fitting may be associated with the fuel plumbing that connected the tank to the aircraft. The tapered cylindrical form, horizontal seam, and circular fitting support the identification as an aircraft drop tank. We are unable to determine the circumstances by which the tank entered Lake Union. 

Prior Research and Theories
Previously, Coastal Sensing & Survey had classified this target as LU73. Described as a kayak.

Additional Context
Aircraft drop tanks are external fuel tanks designed to extend an aircraft's range and could be released when no longer needed. They were expendable by nature and made from a lightweight construction. Post World War II aircraft drop tanks were used for other purposes such as floats, small sail boats, and racecars. Shipwreck City is actively researching this object's history and will provide more details as we learn more.
